hour noun

also o’clock, telling the time, half past, time, every hour, hourly, from hour to hour, at two o’clock

classical

Traupman 80–81
Plin. Ep. 3.1.4: hōrā secundā calceōs poscit
Gell. 3.2.16: ā sextā noctis hōrā
Traupman 330
Traupman 394

hōra, hōrae f.

noun, first declension

A Roman hour was a twelfth of the time from sunrise to sunset, so it was longer in summer than in winter: hōra prīma was the first hour after sunrise, hōra sexta ended at noon and hōra duodecima at sunset; the night had twelve hours of its own, and midnight was sexta noctis hōra (Gell. 3.2.16). The modern way puts the same words on our clock (Traupman 80–81): prīma hōra is one o’clock, with ante merīdiem or post merīdiem where needed; the twenty-four hours can be counted too (hōrā ūndēvīcēsimā, at 7 p.m.). So hōrā nōnā is 9 a.m. on our clock but mid-afternoon on the Roman one.

Examples

  • hōrā nōnā et sēmihōrā

    at 9:30composed

  • māne lectulō continētur, hōrā secundā calceōs poscit, ambulat mīlia passuum tria

    in the morning he stays in bed; at the second hour (the Roman way, counted from sunrise) he calls for his shoes and walks three milesPlin. Ep. 3.1.4

  • Est secunda hōra.

    It’s two o’clock (the modern way).Traupman 81

  • Hōrā septimā et sēmihōrā.

    At half past seven.Traupman 81

  • singulīs hōrīs

    every hourTraupman 87

  • clāvum mūtāre in hōrās

    to change his stripe every hourHor. S. 2.7.10 (Lewis & Short s.v. hōra)

  • hōrā diēī secundā

    at two o’clock (literally “at the second hour of the day”)Traupman 353

  • in hōrās

    hourly, from hour to hourTraupman 330
